[PAPER_0061, relevance_score=0.296] We hypothesize that attention capture costs, measured via the difference of RTs between distractor present and distractor absent trials, will negatively correlate with both working memory capacity and attention control (contrary to Robison & Unsworth, 2017 which only found a correlation between attention capture and working memory, and not attention control). We also hypothesize that oculometric indicators of attention capture, like dwell time on the distractor and distraction probability, will positively correlate with the RT effect.

[PAPER_0062, relevance_score=0.253] We predict these indicators will negatively correlate with working memory capacity and attention control, such that those with the greatest search efficiency and least probability for distraction will have higher working memory and attention control scores. We also test whether pupillary measures of attentional intensity and consistency (Miller et al., 2019; Unsworth & Miller, 2021) will positively correlate with working memory capacity and attention control but negatively correlate with individual differences in attention capture.

[PAPER_0063, relevance_score=0.347] Method

Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, and all measures in the study. The study's design and hypotheses were preregistered on the Open Science Framework and can be found as the additional online materials (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/ysvu5). Data and analysis scripts are publicly available and can be found as the additional online materials (https://osf.io/6xbac).

[PREREG_0002, relevance_score=0.342] Finally, correlations among the measures and external measures of attention control and working memory capacity will be examined.

q2: Hypothesis 1: Attention capture costs, measured via reaction time, will negatively correlate with working memory capacity and attention control.

Hypothesis 2: Attention capture costs, measured via reaction time, will positively correlate with oculometric indicators of attention capture.

Hypothesis 3: Oculometric indicators of attention capture will negatively correlate with working memory capacity and attention control.

[PREREG_0003, relevance_score=0.370] Hypothesis 4: Pupillary measures of attentional intensity will positively correlate with working memory capacity and attention control, and negatively correlate with RT measures of attention capture.

Hypothesis 5: Pupillary measures of attentional consistency will positively correlate with working memory capacity and attention control, and negatively correlate with RT measures of attention capture.

[PREREG_0020, relevance_score=0.374] We expect there to be at least one coherent factor derived from the oculometric data, which will indicate visual search efficiency (e.g., longer time to fixate on target, more saccades on non-targets before target fixation) and/or overt visual attention capture by a singleton (proportion of distractor-present trials in which the singleton is fixated) Once these factors are identified, we will use the predict() function in lavaan to extract factor scores, and these will be correlated with the behavior indices of attention capture (Hypothesis 2) and the WMC and AC factor scores (Hypothesis 3).

[PREREG_0022, relevance_score=0.322] Specifically, we hypothesize that larger pupillary responses will correlate with higher WMC, better AC, lower attention capture, and better visual search efficiency.

We will then compute the intraindividual mean and intraindividual standard deviation of pretrial pupil diameter for each participant, and this value will be correlated with the WMC and AC factor scores, the attention capture RT effect, and the oculometric factors (Hypothesis 5).

[PREREG_0023, relevance_score=0.305] Specifically, we hypothesize that less intraindividual variability in pretrial pupil diameter will correlate with higher WMC, better AC, lower attention capture, and better visual search efficiency.

[PAPER_0099, relevance_score=0.371] Exclusions

For behavioral data, we excluded participants had accuracy less than 75% to remove those who were likely to be guessing. For the remaining participants, RTs shorter than 200 ms and longer than 3,000 ms were removed (Bacon & Egeth, 1994; Folk et al., 1994; Robison & Unsworth, 2017; Theeuwes, 1992).

[PAPER_0100, relevance_score=0.395] For the eye-tracking gaze data, we excluded trials on which more than 50% of data was missing or invalid, and then participants who had more than 50% of trials excluded (60 trials).3 For pupil diameter data, we excluded pupil diameters outside 1 and 9 mm since these are outside the physiological range for pupil size (Mathôt et al., 2018), and we again excluded trials that had more than 50% data missing and excluded participants who had more than 50% trials missing.

[PAPER_0101, relevance_score=0.473] We followed the same exclusion criteria for pretrial pupil data (n = 205). For all variables, we used a multipass outlier screening for z-score values that fell ±3 SDs outside the mean. The number of passes and number removed for each variable are presented in the descriptive tables.
